Grace Notes and Ornaments: How to Play Them

The ornament tables of Bach, Couperin, Geminiani, Purcell, Türk, Leopold Mozart, Clementi and Hummel, read from the original prints, each sign written and played out; Haydn and Mozart in practice, Chopin and the 19th century, Irish ornaments, and jazz and blues chart symbols, with reference recordings.

A grace note is a small note printed before a main note. An ornament is a sign (a trill, a mordent, a turn) that stands for a short group of notes. Neither tells you exactly when the extra notes sound or how long they last. The answer depends on the period and the style, and for older music it comes from what performers and teachers of the time wrote down.

The main question is the same in every style: does the grace note fall on the beat, taking time from the main note, or just before the beat, taking time from the note before?

Many composers and teachers answered that question in print, in tables of their signs with the notes written out underneath. This page gives eight of those tables as their authors wrote them, read from the original prints and manuscripts, from Bach (1720) to Hummel (1828), alongside how the signs were used in practice, and the very different habits of Irish traditional music and of jazz and blues.

How to use the page. Each sign is shown twice: as written, and played out the way the source writes it, moved onto the note C so the tables can be compared. Press ▶ on either to hear the played-out notes. Small print under a name gives the page in the source, and says where a note count or rhythm is our reading rather than the source’s. Each part ends with recordings to hear the style. The Classical Themes page plays grace notes on the beat, the Baroque and Classical default.

Two kinds of grace note

Written Name Where it falls How long
small note, no slash appoggiatura on the beat long: often half the main note, or more
small note with a slash acciaccatura on or just before the beat as short as possible

The slash only became a reliable sign in the 19th century. In Bach and Haydn an unslashed small note can still be short, and the context decides (Neumann, Ornamentation in Baroque; Rosenblum).

Bach and the Baroque

In 1720 J. S. Bach wrote a table of ornaments, the Explication, at the front of the keyboard book he began for his son Wilhelm Friedemann. Each sign stands above a quarter note with the notes it stands for written out below (Bach, Clavier-Büchlein). Together with C. P. E. Bach’s Versuch (1753) and Quantz (1752), it is the main evidence for how Bach’s signs were played.

Bach’s whole table

Here is the Explication entry by entry, each on the note C as Bach wrote it: the sign, and the notes Bach wrote out beneath it, with his own note values, read from the manuscript (Bach, Clavier-Büchlein, leaf 3v). Both ▶ buttons in a row play the same written-out notes.

Bach’s values do not always add up to the quarter note above them: the trill and the mordent stop short, and the last three entries run over. The table shows the shape of each ornament, not a count. On a longer note or at a slower tempo a trill goes on longer, and its last note is held (Neumann, Ornamentation in Baroque).

His signs differ in small hooks and strokes that the music font here cannot draw:

  • Trillo: a short wave of two humps. Mordant: a short wave with a vertical stroke through it. Trillo und Mordant: a longer wave ending in that stroke.
  • Cadence: a curl standing upright, like a question mark, not the lying ∽ used today.
  • Doppelt-Cadence: a small hook rising from below into the wave (begin below). Idem: a large hook coming down from above (begin with a turn from above). Entries 7 and 8 add the closing stroke.
  • Accent: a small hook just before the note; the realisation shows whether it rises or falls.
  • The last Idem: a stroke dropping into a long wave.
# Bach's name Sign Played
1 Trillo
trill
Bach's values: five 32nds and a dotted 32nd, short of the quarter; the trill fills the note.
2 Mordant
mordent
Written as two 32nds and a dotted 32nd; the main note is then held.
3 Trillo und Mordant
trill ending with a mordent
4 Cadence
turn
Four 32nds, as Bach wrote them.
5 Doppelt-Cadence
trill from the note below
6 Idem
trill from a turn above
7 Doppelt-Cadence und Mordant
from below, ending with a mordent
8 Idem
from a turn above, on a dotted note, ending with a mordent

Hear it. The Netherlands Bach Society’s All of Bach videos are free and well made. Two show Bach writing ornaments out in full, the best evidence of what his signs meant:

  • English Suite No. 2, BWV 807, Bertrand Cuiller: the Sarabande at 11:32, then Bach’s own ornamented version, Les agréments de la même Sarabande, at 14:16.
  • Italian Concerto, BWV 971, Christine Schornsheim: the Andante, whose melody Bach wrote out ornament by ornament, at 4:22.
  • English Suite No. 3, BWV 808, Pierre Hantaï: the Sarabande at 10:23.
  • Goldberg Variations, BWV 988, Jean Rondeau: the Aria, almost every beat ornamented.

The appoggiatura: on the beat, and long

An appoggiatura is played on the beat and takes its length from the main note. C. P. E. Bach’s rule: before a note that divides in two it takes half, and before a dotted note it takes two thirds (C. P. E. Bach, ch. 2, sec. 2). It is the dissonant note, so it is the louder one, and the main note resolves it softly.

Not every scholar agrees that all of Bach’s small notes are long and on the beat. Frederick Neumann argued that many, especially those filling in a falling third, were short and could come before the beat (Neumann, Ornamentation in Baroque). Treat on the beat as the default, and use a short or pre-beat grace when the long one would spoil the line or the counterpoint.

The trill: start on the upper note

Bach’s table and C. P. E. Bach both start a trill on the note above, on the beat, so the trill begins with a dissonance like an appoggiatura. A trill on a long note may end with a turn (Nachschlag) into the next note.

The mordent: main note, the one below, main note

Bach’s mordant is quick: the main note, the note below, then back, all at the start of the beat.

Improvising ornaments

Baroque players were expected to add ornaments of their own, above all on the repeat of a slow movement. Bach shows how far this could go: after the Sarabande of his English Suite No. 3 he wrote out a second, ornamented version of the whole tune, Les agréments de la même Sarabande. Below is its opening theme (from the Classical Themes collection), followed by two ways to ornament it that a Baroque player might choose, and one they would not.

Choice 1, French: graces on the strong notes. An appoggiatura from above leans on beat 2, where a sarabande puts its weight. A trill from the upper note goes on the leading tone, and a mordent goes on the last note of the cadence. The tune stays the same, and each ornament falls on a note that is a dissonance or a point of arrival.

Choice 2, Italian: fill in the long notes. The long notes are broken into running notes (passaggi, also called divisions) that circle the written pitch and move on to the next one. The notes that fall on the beat are still the written melody, so the harmony underneath doesn’t change. Corelli’s slow movements, printed with ornaments added in 1710, are the classic model.

Not appropriate: ornaments everywhere, and on the wrong notes. Here there’s a mordent on every note, and a trill on the final G, where the cadence comes to rest. A trill adds tension, so it belongs on the note before the resolution, never on the resolution itself. With an ornament on every note, beat 2 no longer stands out, and the dance goes with it. C. P. E. Bach warned that ornaments used too freely are like too much seasoning (C. P. E. Bach, ch. 2, sec. 1).

France: Couperin and d’Anglebert

The French harpsichordists printed the most detailed ornament tables of all, and Bach’s own table borrows from them. Jean-Henri d’Anglebert’s Pièces de clavecin (1689) opens with 29 agréments: plain, leaned-on and turned trills (tremblement simple, appuyé, cadence), the double cadence (a turn), the pincé (mordent), the cheute or port de voix (appoggiatura from below or above), coulés filling in thirds, arpeggios, and the détaché, a short silence before a trill or a mordent. Like Bach, he writes every ornament on the beat and starts every trill from the note above (d’Anglebert).

François Couperin’s L’Art de toucher le clavecin (1716) explains how his signs are played, and adds two things the tables do not show. A trill’s beats “begin more slowly than they end”, and every pincé, double pincé and trill stops on the main note (the point d’arrêt) inside the note’s value (Couperin).

# Couperin's name Sign Played
1 Pincé simple
mordent: the note below once, then the note held
Written in small notes; their exact length is not given.
2 Pincé double
a longer mordent, stopping on the note (point d'arrêt) inside its value
3 Port de voix
the small note below "strikes with the harmony": on the beat; here with a pincé
4 Tremblement
always from the note or semitone above: the appui (leaned on), the beats (starting slower than they end), the point d'arrêt
The beats speed up; even notes here. The length of the appui is left to the player.

Italy and England: Geminiani and Purcell

Francesco Geminiani’s The Art of Playing on the Violin (London, 1751) lists fourteen “Ornaments of Expression” and, unusually, says what each one expresses: a long beat for “Fury, Anger, Resolution”, a soft swelling one for “Horror, Fear, Grief”. Six of them change the notes; the rest are holding the note, staccato, swelling and diminishing, piano and forte, and the “close shake”, which he says “cannot possibly be described by Notes” (it is vibrato, and he wants it often) (Geminiani).

# Geminiani's name Sign Played
1 A plain Shake
Trillo semplice: for quick movements
Eight slurred 32nds; the start on the note above is read from the group ending on the main note.
2 A turn'd Shake
Trillo composto: quick and long for gaiety, short and soft for tender passions
About ten notes on the plate: the trill, the note below, the main note.
3 A superior Apogiatura
from above, on the beat, "more than half the Length" of the note, swelling
Geminiani gives it more than half the note; the plate also shows a short one.
4 An inferior Apogiatura
from the note below, only when the melody rises a second or third, then a beat
5 Holding the Note
Trattenimento: the note held plain, then shaken, so the pure note is heard
Shape from the plate; note count approximate.
6 A Beat
the note and the semitone below, slurred: strong and long for fury, soft and swelling for grief
A trill on the lower note, starting on the main note.

Henry Purcell’s harpsichord Lessons (1696, published by his widow) begin with “Rules for Graces”: “you allway’s shake from the note above and beat from ye note or half note below, according to the key you play in”. A shake is the upper-note trill; a beat is the English name for a mordent from the note below. The printed examples are hard to read and are said to contain misprints, so the note counts below follow the rules more than the plate (Purcell).

# Purcell's name Sign Played
1 Shake
from the note above ("you allway's shake from the note above")
The sign is a double oblique stroke through the stem.
2 Beat
from the note or half note below, "according to the key you play in"
A stroke with a cross stroke. The rule is clear; the number of notes on the poor scan is not.
3 Plain note and Shake
half the note held on the note above, then shaken (a dotted note: only the dot)
4 Forefall
an oblique stroke rising to the note: the note below first
5 Backfall
a stroke falling to the note: the note above first

Haydn, Mozart and the Classical style

The Classical sources keep the long appoggiatura on the beat but give the short one more room. Leopold Mozart’s violin method (1756) and Türk’s Klavierschule (1789) both describe long appoggiaturas that take half or more of the main note, and short ones that are played quickly on the beat, taking only a sliver of the main note (L. Mozart; Türk, ch. 3).

  • Long or short? A small note written as a longer value (an eighth before a quarter) is usually long. A sixteenth or a thirty-second before a note, a grace before a repeated note, or one in a quick tempo is usually short (Türk; Neumann, Mozart).
  • On the beat. Even the short ones fall on the beat in Haydn and Mozart, with the bass. Playing them before the beat is a later habit (Brown).
  • Trills. Most begin on the upper note, as in Bach, but Classical sources allow a main-note start when the note before is already the upper note, or when the trill starts a phrase (Rosenblum; Neumann, Mozart).

Three treatises, as their authors wrote them

Daniel Gottlob Türk’s Klavierschule (1789), Leopold Mozart’s violin method (1756) and Muzio Clementi’s piano Introduction (c. 1801) are the closest we have to Bach’s table for Haydn’s and Mozart’s world. All three put the appoggiatura on the beat and give it half the main note (more before a dotted note), and all start the trill on the note above. They differ in the details: Türk times the short appoggiatura by tempo; Leopold Mozart lets an appoggiatura before a dotted note take everything but the dot, and allows one grace before the beat, the passing appoggiatura between notes a third apart; Clementi, a generation later, allows a short shake that starts on the main note, and says composers leave the kind of shake to “the taste and judgment of the performer” (Türk; L. Mozart; Clementi).

Türk, Klavierschule (1789)

Haydn’s own sign

Haydn’s keyboard music has a sign of its own, a turn with a vertical stroke through it, the “Haydn ornament”. What it meant is still argued over, and the sources disagree even on where it stands: in the slow movement of the E♭ Sonata, Hob. XVI:49 (1790), the first edition (Artaria, 1791) engraves a small cross-like sign over two notes in each of bars 9 and 11, where Haydn’s autograph has a sign that a coarse scan cannot tell from a short trill (Haydn, autograph; Haydn, Artaria). Modern editions and Somfai’s study discuss it; until we have read them, this page gives no realisation (Somfai).

Hear four readings of the same Adagio. Hob. XVI:49, II. Adagio e cantabile, on official uploads. Listen to bars 1-12 (about the first minute) and compare the small notes and signs:

  • Ronald Brautigam, fortepiano: YouTube
  • Alfred Brendel, piano: YouTube
  • Paul Lewis, piano: YouTube
  • Marc-André Hamelin, piano: YouTube

Mozart writes it out

Mozart’s Sonata in F, K. 332, shows how much a Classical player added. In the autograph, the Adagio’s reprise repeats the opening plainly; in the first edition (Artaria, 1784), printed under Mozart’s eye, the same bars return heavily embellished, with runs of 32nds, triplets and trills (Mozart, Artaria). Hear it on fortepiano: Kristian Bezuidenhout, K. 332, II. Adagio; the reprise comes about halfway through.

Hummel, Chopin and the 19th century

Through the 19th century, short grace notes moved before the beat in much music, and trills more and more started on the main note (Brown). The turning point in print is Johann Nepomuk Hummel’s piano method (1828). He says the old rule, the trill from the note above, “was made for the voice”, and that on the piano the weight belongs on the main note: his trill begins and ends on it, and a start from above or below has to be written as a small note (Hummel).

# Hummel's name Written Played
1 Triller
trill: "begins with the main note and always ends with it too", with a closing turn as fast as the trill
p. 394: the upper-note start "was made for the voice"; on the piano the weight belongs on the main note.
2 Triller von oben
a start from above must be shown by a small added note
3 Triller von unten
and a start from below likewise
4 Schneller
a short trill: main, upper, main, quick and on the beat
p. 398; note values approximate.
5 Doppelschlag von oben
turn from the note above, "lively, round and rather strong"
pp. 398-399.
6 Doppelschlag von der Hauptnote

7 Doppelschlag von unten

Chopin is the exception pianists remember. His pupils report that he wanted grace notes and the start of trills played with the bass note, on the beat (Eigeldinger). The Polish National Edition’s performance notes spell it out piece by piece: in the Moderato in E (WN 56) the first grace note is struck with the bass; “all trills without grace notes should begin with the principal”; and where Chopin writes a small note before a trill, the trill starts on that note, “simultaneously with the G in the left hand”. Yet in the early Contredanse (WN 27) the edition says to “execute all grace notes in an anticipated manner”, before the beat (Ekier). Chopin wanted even a turn sung: “not a quick gruppetto, but eight notes well sung” (Ekier). Raoul Pugno, who studied the Chopin tradition in Paris, notes that in the Berceuse a small flat over a trill belongs to its upper note, and asks for two of its trills “a little longer” and the next one strictly in time (Pugno).

Singers kept the older rule longest. Manuel García’s Traité (1847) says the appoggiatura in Italian singing is less an ornament than a matter of the words: it “falls always on the downbeat and on the long syllable”, and can come from any interval, a fifth in Mozart’s “andiam” in Don Giovanni (García).

Hear it. Recordings by players and singers trained in the 19th century, free on the Internet Archive:

  • Vladimir de Pachmann, Chopin, Nocturne in B, Op. 32 No. 1 and Mazurka in F♯ minor (1912, Library of Congress National Jukebox).
  • Ignacy Jan Paderewski, Chopin, Nocturne in F♯, Op. 15 No. 2 (HMV, 1928; the archive’s title says “E sharp”).
  • Adelina Patti, Bellini, “Casta diva” (1906), with more of her 1905–06 recordings: bel canto appoggiaturas and turns from a singer born in 1843.

Irish traditional music

In Irish flute, whistle and fiddle music grace notes are not melody notes at all but articulations: a cut is a flick to a higher note, a tap (or strike) a flick to a lower one, and a roll combines them around a long note. They are so short that they have no rhythmic value of their own and fall right at the start of the main note (Larsen).

Jazz and blues

Jazz players use grace notes freely and they are rarely written. They come before the beat or across it, in swing time, and they are part of how a phrase is shaped rather than decoration added on top. Where an arranger does write them, the big-band chart has its own set of signs: Michele Caniato’s checklist of “expressive devices” runs from gliss, rip and bend through shake, doit, growl, smear, fall, spill and plop to the turn (Caniato).

  • The blue third. On piano, which cannot bend a note, the minor third is crushed into the major third: struck together and the lower one let go, or a quick grace from the minor into the major. It stands in for the singer’s or guitarist’s bend between them (Komara; Hines). Grace from below, never from above, or it sounds minor. See Blues Piano.
  • Terminal vibrato. Louis Armstrong starts a long note straight and lets vibrato in towards its end; Gunther Schuller calls the trumpet shake “a more extreme way of enlivening and swinging the tone” (Schuller). B.B. King’s guitar version is the “butterfly” vibrato, from the wrist (Koch).
  • Ghost notes and bends are written as a note in brackets (or an x notehead) and as an arrow marked ¼, ½ or full.

In the table below, ▶ plays the slides on a clean electric guitar, so a fall falls and a bend bends, where notation can only show steps. How far and how fast each one goes is our estimate: players differ.

# Name In a chart Roughly played
1 Crushed note
piano: the minor and major third struck together, the lower let go at once, standing in for a bend
Komara; Hines, ed. Taylor.
2 Fall
a line falling away after the note: at the release, never before the beat, into silence
3 Doit
the opposite: "a smear that ascends into infinity after the initial pitch is heard"
Pejrolo and DeRosa.
4 Scoop
a curve up into the note: the attack is on the beat but below pitch, sliding up
5 Plop
a curve down into the note from above
6 Rip
a fast run up from below, starting before the beat so the top note lands on it
7 Bend
guitar: push the string up a whole step ("full"; ½ = a half step), hold, let it back down
8 Shake
trumpet: a wide, fast lip trill, "done solely with the embouchure"
Pejrolo and DeRosa; Barnhart.
9 Enclosure
bebop: the notes above and below circle the target, which lands on the beat
Usually written out in full; a bebop staple (Owens).

Hear it. Official uploads (label channels):

  • Louis Armstrong and His Hot Five, “West End Blues” (1928): the opening cadenza, then bends and the blue third in the first strain and “hushed vibrato on the final A♭” (Edexcel).
  • Meade “Lux” Lewis, “Honky Tonk Train Blues” and Jimmy Yancey, “Yancey Stomp”: crushed notes.
  • Thelonious Monk Quartet, “Misterioso”: crushed minor seconds (Kelley).
  • Count Basie Orchestra, “April in Paris” (1955): falls and shakes from the whole band.
  • Duke Ellington, “Black and Tan Fantasy” (1927): growl and plunger, smears.
  • Charlie Parker, “Ko-Ko” and “Parker’s Mood”: bebop turns and enclosures, blues inflection on alto.
  • B.B. King, “The Thrill Is Gone” (1969): bends and butterfly vibrato.
  • Billie Holiday, “Strange Fruit” (1939): late placement and sparing vibrato (Gourse).

J. S. Bach (1720) on the beat, long by default upper note J. S. Bach; C. P. E. Bach; Neumann
d’Anglebert, Couperin (1689, 1716) on the beat (“with the harmony”) upper note, leaned on, beats speeding up d’Anglebert; Couperin
Purcell (1696) forefall / backfall on the beat “from the note above”; beat from below Purcell
Geminiani (1751) on the beat, more than half the note upper note Geminiani
Leopold Mozart (1756) on the beat, half (all but the dot before a dotted note); passing ones before upper note L. Mozart
Türk (1789) on the beat; short ones a 32nd at moderate speed upper note, even Türk
Clementi (c. 1801) on the beat, “in general” half upper note; a short shake may start on the note Clementi
Hummel (1828) half the note, on the beat; short ones almost nothing main note Hummel
Chopin with the bass, on the beat main note unless a small note says otherwise Eigeldinger; Ekier
Later 19th century short ones before the beat main note Brown
Irish traditional a flick at the start of the note (rolls, not trills) Larsen
Jazz, blues before or across the beat, swung (shakes, falls, doits) Caniato; Komara; Schuller
